Why Laboratory Safety Matters

Safe working protects you, other lab workers, cleaners, visitors, your work and the environment.

Implementing a lab health and safety program is mandatory to avoid:

  • Injury, death or disablements.
  • Work disruption.
  • Loss of valuable equipment or records.
  • Damage to the lab, building or the environment.

General hazards in a laboratory

  • Fire
  • Breakage of glassware
  • Sharps
  • Spillages
  • Pressure equipment and gas cylinders
  • Extremes of heat and cold
  • Chemical hazards
  • Biological hazards
  • Radiation

Assessing Risk and Hazards

There is always risk. It must be identified, evaluated, and a plan made to minimize it.

Identify risk
Evaluate risk
Plan to minimize
Definition

A laboratory safety plan is a written document that identifies the hazards that may be encountered and specifies practices and procedures to eliminate or minimize exposure to biohazardous materials.

Risk assessment has two parts: identifying the hazards and choosing the control measures.

Hazards

  • Physical: needles, glass, fire, electricity, UV radiation.
  • Chemical: acids, alkalis.
  • Biological agents: clinical samples, microbial cultures.

Biohazardous materials

Biohazardous materials are hazardous biological materials and organisms, including:

  • Infectious organisms.
  • Human or primate tissues, fluids, cells, or cell culture.
  • Recombinant DNA.
  • Animals known to be vectors of zoonotic diseases.

Control Measures

Control measurePrincipleExamples
Engineering controlsRemove or separate the hazard from the personLocal ventilation (fume hoods); biological safety cabinets (BSCs)
Administrative controlsProcedures that limit contact with the hazardStandard operating procedures (SOPs); staff training; good housekeeping
Work practicesSafe and proper work procedures that reduce the duration, frequency and intensity of exposureNo eating or drinking in the lab; laboratory hygiene rules
Personal protective equipment (PPE)Barrier worn by the workerLab coat, gloves, goggles, face shield, rubber apron

Personal protective equipment

The lab coat must be worn properly. Minimum recommended PPE: chemical-resistant gloves, splash-proof goggles, lab coat, face shield, and a rubber apron when necessary.

Work practices and laboratory hygiene

  • No eating or drinking in the lab, and no chewing gum or anything else that goes in the mouth.
  • Never apply cosmetics.
  • Never touch your face, mouth or eyes.
  • Never suck pens or chew pencils.
  • Always wash your hands before you leave and especially before eating.
  • Labeling of chemicals and solutions is important.

Storage and Chemical Safety

Storage and housekeeping

  • Store flammables in a flammables cabinet.
  • Store acids in an acid cabinet.
  • Avoid overhead storage.
  • Avoid desk clutter, floor clutter and shelf clutter.

Handling chemicals

  • Never mix chemicals together unless told to do so, and then only in the manner specified.
  • Never taste any chemicals (never taste anything in the lab).
  • To smell a chemical, waft the fumes toward your nose with one hand; do not put your nose over the container and inhale.
  • Read labels carefully. NFPA diamonds and HMIS bars are colour- and number-coded with hazard information; DOT symbols are usually found on shipping cartons.
High-yield

Never pour water into a concentrated acid. Pour the acid slowly into water.

Chemical inventory

Conduct a yearly inventory of chemicals and update the file of material safety data sheets (MSDS). This prevents the accumulation of orphaned chemicals, which may become unstable, react with the container, slowly degrade or evaporate.

Labeling biological material

Biological material that others may have access to (such as cultures) should be labeled with what the content is and any precautions. Example: Escherichia coli requires eye protection, lab coat and gloves, and must only be used under a biological safety cabinet.

Fire, Glassware, Spills, Electrical and Waste

Fire safety

  • Know what to do if you have a fire and if you hear a fire alarm.
  • Fire extinguishers must be accessible and maintained.
  • Lab members must be trained on how to use them.

Glassware

  • Do not use chipped or cracked glassware.
  • Dispose of broken glassware in a special glass disposal container.
  • When pouring liquids into glassware, the container being poured into should rest on a table at least a handsbreadth from the edge.
  • Do not place hot glassware in water; rapid cooling may make it shatter.

Spillages

  • Clear up spillage promptly, in the way determined as part of the risk assessment.
  • Dispose of any hazardous material as toxic waste.
  • Messy workers are usually poor workers.

Electrical equipment

  • Always do a visual check before use, looking for obvious wear or defects.
  • All portable electrical equipment must have a current "PAT test" sticker.
  • Never use defective equipment.

Waste materials

  • How to dispose of waste lab materials safely is part of the risk assessment.
  • Solvents and oils must be segregated into the correct waste bottle or drum.
  • Your department helps determine what to do with chemical or biological materials.
  • Do not put materials down the drain or in with normal waste unless authorised to do so.
  • Biological waste must be disposed of properly.

Emergency First Aid

Laboratories need first aid equipment and trained lab staff.

  • Burns: immediately flush with cold water until the burning sensation is lessened.
  • Cuts and bruises: do not touch an open wound without safety gloves. Pressing directly on minor cuts stops bleeding in a few minutes. Apply a cold compress to bruises to reduce swelling.
  • The eyes: flush immediately with plenty of water for several minutes. If a foreign object is lodged in the eye, do not allow the eye to be rubbed.
  • Poisoning: find out what substance was responsible and alert the teacher immediately.
  • Spills on the skin: flush with large quantities of water. Apply baking soda solution for acid spills; vinegar or boric acid for base spills.
  • Electrical shock: shut off the current at the source. Remove the wire with rubber gloves. Alert the teacher immediately.

Key Terms

Check yourself

Which control measures remove or separate the hazard from the person?

Engineering controls, such as fume hoods and biological safety cabinets.

How should a concentrated acid be diluted?

Pour the acid slowly into water; never pour water into a concentrated acid.

What is applied to an acid spill on the skin after flushing with water?

Baking soda solution (vinegar or boric acid is used for base spills).

Key Points / Quick Review

Purpose and risk

  • A lab safety program is mandatory to avoid injury, work disruption, loss of equipment or records, and damage to lab or environment.
  • Risk is identified, evaluated and minimized; the lab safety plan is a written document.
  • Hazards are physical, chemical or biological.

Control measures and PPE

  • Engineering: fume hoods, BSCs.
  • Administrative: SOPs, training, housekeeping.
  • Minimum PPE: chemical-resistant gloves, splash-proof goggles, lab coat, face shield, rubber apron when necessary.

Hygiene

  • No eating, drinking or cosmetics; do not touch face, mouth or eyes.
  • Never suck pens or chew pencils.
  • Wash hands before leaving and before eating.

Storage and chemicals

  • Flammables cabinet; acid cabinet; avoid overhead storage and clutter.
  • Never mix or taste chemicals; waft to smell.
  • Acid into water, never water into concentrated acid.
  • Yearly inventory and updated MSDS file.

Fire, glass, electrical, waste

  • Keep extinguishers accessible and train staff.
  • No chipped glass; no hot glass in water.
  • Current PAT sticker; never use defective equipment.
  • Segregate solvents and oils; no drain disposal unless authorised.

First aid

  • Burns and eyes: flush with water.
  • Skin spills: large quantities of water; baking soda for acid, vinegar or boric acid for base.
  • Electrical shock: shut off the current at the source.
